issues.item: Rumination: Self-Blame: repeatedly blame myself for what happened
issues.explanation: The self-blame item is not clinically supported elsewhere in the profile. There are no Negative Appraisal or Memory items indicating guilt, responsibility, shame, or a trauma narrative that would make repeated self-blame coherent. With this formulation, the only strong cycle is Threat ↔ Maladaptive Strategies, so maladaptive strategies should plausibly function to manage current danger/safety concerns. Drug use and avoiding thinking fit that threat-management loop, but repeated self-blame instead implies an unrepresented negative-appraisal process and sits weakly with the rest of the selected items.

vignette: Sanjay, a 31‑year‑old carpenter from the South‑East of the United States, was working late on a kitchen renovation in a suburban home when the alarm for a nearby police raid rattled his thoughts. The siren’s wail was followed by the sudden arrival of a squad of officers who, on the street corner, had a confrontation with a small group of teenagers. Sanjay, passing by, heard a gunshot echo through the street and felt a sharp, immediate sense of danger. In the heat of the moment he ducked into the corner of a vacant lot and, instinctively, pressed his back against a concrete wall, feeling that the wall was the only line of defense against an unseen threat. From that instant the feeling of threat dominated Sanjay’s experience. The image of the police’s flashlights and the echo of gunfire made him hyper‑alert: he could not relax even in the safety of his own house. Whenever a simple delay—like a delayed delivery of plywood—loomed, he automatically assumed that something bad was about to happen. The threat he felt in that moment propelled him into rumination, self‑blame, drug use, and avoidance of thinking. He would lie awake, replaying the gunshot, blaming himself for not having been more attentive or for not having stayed inside. To numb the relentless anxiety he began using alcohol and prescription painkillers, seeking the brief relief of a numbed mind. Yet the more he avoided thinking about the event, the deeper his anxiety grew, as he was unable to process the memory and to contextualise the threat that now haunted his every pause. His maladaptive coping only magnified his sense of threat, causing him to cling to walls and to view everyday delays as imminent danger. Whenever he walked into a shop for a hammer or a new batch of nails, the mere act of crossing the threshold triggered a surge of fear. His use of drugs, instead of providing relief, heightened his sensitivity to sound and movement, so that even the hum of a refrigerator in his kitchen sounded like a police radio. The rumination he engaged in at night was not merely a way of coping; it was a rehearsal of the terror that had begun in that vacant lot. As a result, he could not relax even in the safe confines of his own living room; the threat remained, amplified by his own attempts to evade it. The tightening cycle of threat and maladaptive coping spilled into his daily life. He stopped bringing work equipment into the office space of his small carpentry shop, fearing that the tools might be targeted or that the noise would trigger a police response. When he finally had to meet a client, he avoided eye contact, staying near a wall as he described, so he could keep his back “against a wall” at all times. The delays in his usual schedule became a source of dread: a late shipment of studs or a postponed meeting would cause him to freeze, checking his phone obsessively for updates that never came. At home, his wife noticed his withdrawn mood and his abrupt silences. He would often leave their shared apartment to take a walk, standing in front of the neighbor’s house, keeping his back against a wall, as if the concrete could shield him from the world that now felt hostile. Sanjay’s relentless cycle had begun to erode both his work performance and his marriage. He missed deadlines, leading to costly re‑orders and angry clients, while his wife worried that he was withdrawing from her and the family. He stopped telling her about the incident because he feared that talking about it would invite further threat in the form of judgment or disbelief. The avoidance of thinking about the event became so ingrained that even simple conversations about the day left him feeling unsettled. Finally, the accumulation of stressors reached a breaking point. Sanjay found himself unable to sleep, constantly staring at the ceiling, and unable to focus on his craft. He realized that his life was increasingly dominated by the thought of the gunshot and the feeling that his back had to be pressed against a wall to survive. He decided to seek help because the cycle of threat and maladaptive coping was no longer sustainable. What frightened him most now is the possibility that if he fails to change this pattern, he may lose his job and his relationship entirely. He hopes to find a way to feel safe again, to let his mind move beyond the gunshot, and to rebuild his life without the constant shadow of threat.
